strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting: neural motion fields give good quality but require expensive per-Gaussian deformation inference. The proposed combination of temporal sensitivity pruning and grouped SE(3) motion distillation is well aligned with this bottleneck and has clear potential usefulness.

The empirical results are broad for this area. The authors evaluate on MonoDyGauBench across 50 scenes and also provide detailed SpeeDe3DGS ablations on NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, and HyperNeRF. The reported speedups are substantial: e.g., DeformableGS + pruning reaches 6.78x higher FPS on MonoDyGauBench with small average quality loss, and pruning + GroupFlow reaches 13.71x higher FPS.

The ablations are helpful. The paper separately studies TSP, TSS, GroupFlow, number of motion groups, pruning ratios, Gaussian counts, model size, FPS, and training time. This makes the speed-quality tradeoff more transparent than many efficiency papers.

The method is conceptually simple and likely implementable in existing dynamic 3DGS pipelines. Pruning reduces the primitive count directly, while GroupFlow replaces per-Gaussian neural deformation with shared group transforms; both are plausible, modular acceleration mechanisms.
The paper acknowledges some tradeoffs, especially quality degradation under aggressive pruning and limitations of grouped rigid motion for highly non-rigid regions.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. TSP is largely an adaptation of gradient/sensitivity-based pruning from static 3DGS to dynamic 3DGS, and GroupFlow resembles motion clustering plus rigid transform fitting. The paper’s contribution is mainly an effective engineering combination rather than a fundamentally new representation or theory.

Some technical claims around TSS are not fully justified. The paper states that Eq. 6 requires no ground-truth supervision and that jittered timestamps reveal unstable floaters that receive lower sensitivity scores, but it is not clear how sensitivities at unobserved timestamps are meaningfully computed without a target image/loss signal, nor why the proposed score should consistently downweight floaters. The derivation from second-order loss sensitivity to the implemented pruning score needs more precision.

The quality-preservation claims are somewhat overstated. Several settings show nontrivial degradation: on D-NeRF, pruning drops DeformableGS from 38.92 to 36.19 PSNR and pruning+GroupFlow to 35.07; on MonoDyGauBench, 4DGS+GroupFlow drops from 23.55 to 21.00 PSNR and worsens LPIPS from 0.277 to 0.380. These may be acceptable tradeoffs for speed, but the manuscript sometimes describes fidelity as preserved more strongly than the tables support.

Runtime and training-time comparisons are not perfectly controlled. FPS is measured on RTX 3090, but many reported training times for the proposed methods are measured on RTX A5000 or A6000 while baseline times may come from RTX 3090 or benchmark tables. The paper explains memory constraints, but this still weakens the directness of training-time speedup claims.

Temporal coherence is a central motivation, but the evidence is mostly qualitative or inferred from image metrics. There are no explicit temporal metrics, flicker measurements, trajectory consistency metrics, or user studies, so claims that TSS and GroupFlow improve temporal stability are only partially supported.

Reproducibility could be stronger. The paper gives key hyperparameters such as pruning schedule, beta, tau, and J, but implementation details remain underspecified: exact sensitivity accumulation/normalization, interaction with densification, optimizer settings after GroupFlow initialization, whether group assignments are updated, and the precise training protocol for the cumulative variants.

Some tables and presentation details are confusing. The '+ GroupFlow' label sometimes means GroupFlow alone and sometimes a cumulative pruning+GroupFlow variant depending on the table; several table entries have formatting issues or missing speedup values. These are presentation problems, but they make it harder to audit the experimental evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck in dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting: neural deformation fields can give good reconstruction quality but are slow because they require per-Gaussian inference. Improving this speed/fidelity tradeoff is useful for the community.

The proposed system is simple and practically motivated: temporally aggregated sensitivity pruning reduces primitive count, timestamp perturbation attempts to make pruning more robust, and GroupFlow replaces per-Gaussian neural deformation with shared groupwise SE(3) transforms.

The empirical speedups are large. For DeformableGS on MonoDyGauBench, the paper reports 6.78x faster rendering with pruning and 13.71x with pruning plus GroupFlow, along with shorter training time and roughly 10x fewer Gaussians in several settings.

The evaluation covers several relevant dynamic-view-synthesis datasets and includes ablations over pruning, temporal sampling, GroupFlow, number of groups, pruning percentages, and per-scene metrics in the appendix.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty appears incremental. TSP is a direct extension of existing sensitivity/gradient-based pruning for 3DGS to the temporal case, TSS is timestamp jittering during sensitivity estimation, and GroupFlow is trajectory clustering plus rigid alignment. These are reasonable engineering ideas, but the paper does not convincingly establish a new principle beyond adapting known pruning and grouped-motion concepts to DeformableGS/4DGS.

Several claims about preserving fidelity are overstated. On D-NeRF in the standalone framework, full TSP+TSS+GroupFlow drops from 38.92 to 35.07 PSNR and LPIPS worsens from 0.0143 to 0.0365. On MonoDyGauBench, 4DGS quality drops substantially with the proposed modules, and DeformableGS+GroupFlow worsens LPIPS from 0.283 to 0.313 despite claims of preserving superior image quality. These are meaningful quality tradeoffs, not merely negligible losses.

The evaluation has fairness and interpretability issues. Training times for baselines and proposed methods are sometimes measured on different GPUs, with the proposed methods marked as RTX A5000 while baseline times are on RTX 3090, and HyperNeRF uses A6000 for some training. This weakens the training-speed claims. The paper also mixes results from the standalone SpeeDe3DGS codebase and the MonoDyGauBench wrapper, noting that the standalone code gives better FPS and quality, which makes the headline numbers harder to compare cleanly.

The pruning and TSS methodology is not fully justified. The derivation drops the residual/Hessian term and treats accumulated image-space gradient magnitude as temporal importance, but the paper does not provide enough analysis showing this score reliably identifies redundant or unstable dynamic Gaussians. The claim that TSS detects floaters at unseen timestamps is mostly supported by qualitative examples and small ablation gains; in several tables TSS changes metrics only marginally.

GroupFlow's benefit is partly confounded with regularization and dataset noise. The paper repeatedly claims GroupFlow improves quality by stabilizing noisy poses, but this is not isolated with controlled experiments, pose-noise analysis, temporal metrics, or comparisons to explicit motion regularizers. The method can also fail for non-rigid motion, which is central to the target problem.

Comparisons to related dynamic compression/group-motion methods are incomplete. The related work mentions SC-GS, SPGaussian, RigGS, DynMF, and temporally compressed 3DGS methods, but the experiments mainly compare against MonoDyGauBench baselines rather than directly evaluating against recent methods designed for compact or group-based dynamic Gaussian representations.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Important implementation details such as exact pruning schedule interactions with densification, sensitivity accumulation normalization, sampling counts, memory accounting, and GroupFlow optimization/refinement details are not described at a level that would make independent reproduction straightforward. Code release is not clearly specified.

The manuscript has presentation issues that affect confidence: multiple typos and formatting problems, some table entries appear malformed, and some claims are phrased more strongly than the reported metrics support. These are not the core reason for rejection, but they reinforce the concern that the empirical story is not as clean as presented.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting: neural deformation fields give strong fidelity but require expensive per-Gaussian inference. The proposed combination of temporal sensitivity pruning, timestamp perturbation during pruning, and grouped SE(3) motion distillation is well motivated and practically useful.

The empirical evidence is broad. The authors report results on MonoDyGauBench across 50 scenes and provide additional standalone SpeeDe3DGS experiments on NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, and HyperNeRF, with repeated runs and per-dataset/per-scene appendices.

The main efficiency gains are substantial. For DeformableGS on MonoDyGauBench, pruning improves FPS from 20.20 to 137.01 with almost unchanged aggregate PSNR/SSIM, and adding GroupFlow reaches 276.91 FPS while retaining competitive or improved SSIM/MS-SSIM. The NeRF-DS standalone results similarly show roughly 6-10x rendering speedups with small quality changes.

The paper includes useful ablations for the number of motion groups and pruning percentages, and separately analyzes TSP, TSS, GroupFlow, and their combination. This helps distinguish the source of the gains rather than presenting the method as a single opaque system.

The method is conceptually simple and likely useful as an acceleration module for existing dynamic Gaussian pipelines. The ability to reduce Gaussian counts by around an order of magnitude while preserving much of DeformableGS quality is a meaningful practical contribution.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. TSP is an extension of existing gradient/sensitivity pruning ideas to the temporal setting, TSS is a relatively simple timestamp jittering heuristic, and GroupFlow resembles motion clustering plus rigid alignment/distillation. The value is mainly in the effective integration and empirical validation.

The quality-speed tradeoff is sometimes nontrivial. On MonoDyGauBench, 4DGS+Pruning+GroupFlow drops PSNR from 23.55 to 21.00 and worsens LPIPS from 0.277 to 0.380. In standalone D-NeRF, the full method drops PSNR from 38.92 to 35.07 and LPIPS from 0.0143 to 0.0365. These are acceptable for an efficiency paper but temper the claim of preserving neural-field fidelity across settings.

Training-time comparisons are less clean than FPS comparisons because baseline and proposed training times are sometimes measured on different GPUs, e.g. baseline Train Time on RTX 3090 and proposed Train Time on RTX A5000 in MonoDyGauBench, and HyperNeRF training involving RTX A6000 due to memory. This weakens claims about training acceleration, even though rendering FPS is consistently measured on RTX 3090.

Some methodological details needed for full reproducibility are under-specified. The paper gives pruning schedules and high-level equations, but it is less explicit about exact accumulation/normalization of sensitivities, how soft versus hard pruning interacts with densification, thresholds/tie handling, and the optimization details after GroupFlow initialization.

The justification for TSS is plausible but not fully demonstrated. The paper claims temporal jitter exposes floaters and improves temporal coherence, but evaluation relies mostly on standard image metrics and qualitative examples; explicit temporal stability/flicker metrics would better support this component.

GroupFlow assumes locally rigid shared motion, which is effective in many scenes but can fail for highly non-rigid deformation. The limitation is acknowledged, but the evaluation does not deeply isolate failure cases or characterize when increasing group count cannot recover quality.
